definition: An anti-nausea drug such as ondansetron that blocks serotonin receptors in the gut and brain.
A pathology pattern, either strong diffuse nuclear staining or complete absence, that indicates a TP53 mutation.
Tumor touching a blood vessel over half or less of its circumference on a scan.
US approval granted on a surrogate endpoint such as response rate, with a confirmatory trial expected afterwards.
The enzyme-making cell that forms the bulk of the exocrine pancreas.
A rare pancreatic cancer arising from the enzyme-making acinar cells, with a different course from ductal cancer.
A reversible change in which injured acinar cells take on the appearance and behavior of duct cells.
A tiny rounded cluster of enzyme-making cells around a central duct; thousands of them make up the exocrine pancreas.
A genetic change that points to a specific available or investigational treatment.
A variant of ductal adenocarcinoma in which part of the tumor takes on a squamous, skin-like appearance under the microscope.
Treatment given after surgery to destroy cancer cells that may remain.
Chemotherapy given after surgery to reduce the chance of recurrence.
One particular version of a gene; in this context, which specific KRAS mutation a tumor carries.
How many copies of the mutant gene a cell carries relative to the normal copy.
Extra copies of a gene, which can flood a cell with a growth-driving protein such as HER2.
The small opening in the wall of the duodenum where the bile duct and pancreatic duct empty.
The chamber in the duodenal wall where the bile duct and pancreatic duct open together.
A drug that mimics the hunger hormone ghrelin, approved in Japan but not in the US.
A surgical join between two hollow structures, such as the pancreas and the small intestine.
Too few red blood cells or too little hemoglobin to carry oxygen efficiently.
A lasting unresponsive state a T cell enters when it meets its target without the confirming co-stimulatory signal.
An antibody that recognizes a protein on the cancer cell surface and carries a chemotherapy drug directly to it.
A medicine that slows clotting, taken as tablets or injections.
The lower part of the stomach just before the pylorus, removed in a classic Whipple.
Programmed, orderly self-destruction of a cell that is too damaged to repair.
The number derived from diffusion images that quantifies how freely water moves; low values mean restricted movement.
Free fluid accumulating in the abdominal cavity, often from cancer on the peritoneum.
The alarm kinase that senses a double-strand break and triggers cell-cycle arrest and repair, distinct from the repair enzymes themselves.
Shrinkage of tissue, here of the pancreas upstream of a blocked duct.
A cell's recycling route, in which it wraps part of its own contents in a membrane and delivers the parcel to the lysosome to be broken down into reusable building blocks.
A tumor-cell program resembling squamous epithelium, associated with shorter survival.
The islet cell that makes and releases insulin.
The small partner protein without which MHC class I cannot fold properly or reach the cell surface.
Affecting both copies of a gene, so that no working version remains in the cell.
Loss of both copies of a gene in the tumor, which is what tracks drug sensitivity for these genes.
A yellow-green fluid made by the liver that emulsifies dietary fat and carries bilirubin out of the body.
The yellow pigment produced when old red blood cells are broken down, normally removed from the body in bile.
Raised amylase in drain fluid after surgery without any effect on the patient; not counted as a true fistula.
A single number that lets radiation schedules with different dose sizes and numbers of sessions be compared.
Scan assessment by radiologists who do not know which treatment a patient received and are not part of the treating team.
A dose of drug injected over a few minutes rather than infused over hours.
An extra dose given months after the first course to re-stimulate immune cells that would otherwise fade.
A tumor whose contact with nearby vessels makes a clean surgical margin uncertain; the word refers to removability, not to whether the cancer is malignant.
The most prominent safety warning the FDA places on a drug label.
A point mutation that locks the BRAF kinase on, targetable with a BRAF-plus-MEK inhibitor combination.
An IPMN in a side branch of the duct system, the kind most often found incidentally and most often observed rather than removed.
A core repair gene that loads the RAD51 enzyme onto broken DNA; its loss sensitizes a tumor to platinum and PARP inhibitors.
A US regulatory status that speeds up a drug's review; it describes the process, not evidence that the drug works.
Resistance in which the drug still binds its target but the cell restores the same growth signal through a different route.
A PanIN-like change in normal tissue induced by a nearby tumor rather than being its ancestor.
A sugar structure shed by pancreatic and bile-duct cells into blood, measured as a marker of pancreatic cancer burden in people who can make it.
A fragment of the mucin MUC16 shed by the lining of the abdominal cavity and by some cancers, measured in blood.
A wasting state of ongoing muscle loss driven by the cancer's metabolic signals, not fully reversed by eating more.
A connective-tissue cell within a tumor that has changed state, producing matrix and signals that can either help or restrain the cancer.
A fibroblast living inside a tumor, recruited from the host's own connective tissue rather than derived from the cancer.
Persistent exhaustion out of proportion to activity and not relieved by rest, caused by the cancer or its treatment.
A tablet that the body converts into fluorouracil in three steps, the last of which is more active in tumors.
Cancer-like cells that have not yet broken through the duct wall into surrounding tissue.
Widespread cancer deposits scattered across the peritoneal surface.
The physical, emotional and practical strain on family members providing care.
A receptor on antigen-presenting cells that, when stimulated by an antibody, activates them; in mouse pancreatic tumors the resulting regressions depended on macrophages rather than T cells.
An antibody that pushes rather than blocks, delivering the activating signal antigen-presenting cells need before they can license T cells.
The cytotoxic T cell that can recognize and kill cancer cells.
A specialized dendritic cell that collects material from dying cells and presents it to CD8 T cells in a lymph node, which is the step that starts a killer response.
Kinases that, with cyclin D, release the RB brake and let a cell begin copying its DNA.
Carcinoembryonic antigen, a glycoprotein made by fetal gut and by many adult gut cancers, measured in blood as a tumor marker.
The short arterial trunk from the aorta above the pancreas that divides into the hepatic, splenic and left gastric arteries.
A web of nerves around the celiac artery, in front of the aorta, through which most pain signals from the pancreas travel.
The ordered sequence by which a cell copies its DNA and divides, gated by checkpoints that can halt it.
The normal cell type from which a cancer first arose.
Fragments of DNA, some from the tumor, that circulate in the blood and can be sequenced as a liquid biopsy.
A duct-type cell sitting at the junction between an acinus and its draining duct.
The channel on duct cells that moves chloride and bicarbonate into the duct; it is defective in cystic fibrosis.
A control point that halts the cell cycle until damage is repaired, run largely by p53.
An antibody that blocks a braking receptor such as PD-1 or CTLA-4 on a T cell, releasing a restraint rather than creating a new response.
A checkpoint kinase activated by ATM that helps halt the cell cycle after DNA damage.
A small signaling protein released by tissue that immune cells follow, moving towards wherever its concentration is highest.
A receptor such as CXCR4 or CCR2 that lets an immune cell follow a chemical trail to a particular tissue.
Daily radiation over several weeks combined with a low dose of a chemotherapy drug that makes tumor cells more sensitive to it.
Nerve damage from chemotherapy causing numbness, tingling or pain, usually in the hands and feet.
An artificial receptor that joins an antibody-like gripping part to T-cell signaling parts, so the cell can attack a surface protein without needing a tissue-type molecule.
Bacterial infection of a blocked bile duct, causing fever, chills and jaundice.
A hormone released by the duodenum after a meal that tells acinar cells to release enzymes and the gallbladder to contract.
Any condition in which bile cannot flow from the liver to the intestine.
Watery diarrhea with cramping and sweating within a day of irinotecan, treated with atropine.
DNA wound around histone proteins; its packing determines which genes a cell can read.
A single catastrophic event in which a chromosome shatters and is stitched back together in the wrong order.
Long-standing inflammation of the pancreas, which can raise cancer risk by sustaining tissue damage.
Fragments of DNA shed by cancer cells into the blood, detectable by tests that look for tumor-specific mutations.
The molecular type of pancreatic cancer whose cells most resemble normal duct epithelium.
A scale of complication severity based on the treatment needed, from medication to reoperation or death.
A trial measure combining pain, performance status and weight that must improve and hold for at least four weeks.
Age-related growth of blood-cell clones carrying mutations, which can appear in plasma and mimic tumor DNA.
A group of cells descended from a single ancestor that share its mutations.
The second, confirming signal a T cell needs alongside antigen recognition; without it the cell is switched off rather than switched on.
A three-letter unit of DNA that specifies one amino acid; codons 12, 13 and 61 of KRAS are the cancer hotspots.
The percentage of eaten fat that is absorbed rather than passed in stool.
An unpleasant tingling or tightness triggered by touching or swallowing something cold.
An alternative vein that enlarges to carry blood around a blocked one.
A mucin-rich type of invasive cancer arising from IPMN with a comparatively favorable course.
The branch of the celiac axis that runs along the top of the pancreas toward the liver.
A test the FDA requires to identify who may receive a particular drug.
A broad panel test that reports mutations, copy-number changes, fusions and summary biomarkers together.
A pancreatic cancer that arises elsewhere in the gland, separate from the cyst being watched.
Palliative care delivered at the same time as cancer treatment rather than after it.
The point behind the pancreatic neck where the superior mesenteric vein and splenic vein join to form the portal vein.
A wearable sensor that records blood sugar every few minutes.
A small sensor worn on the skin that measures glucose every few minutes and warns of highs and lows.
One of the timed sets of images taken as injected dye passes through arteries, organs and veins.
An operation performed on a tumor originally judged unresectable after chemotherapy has brought it within reach.
Gain or loss of whole stretches of DNA, as distinct from a single-letter mutation.
A drug that forms a permanent chemical bond with its target protein rather than attaching and detaching.
A metal stent lined with a membrane that blocks tumor ingrowth but can migrate out of place.
The Bayesian equivalent of a confidence interval: the range in which the true effect most plausibly lies given the data.
The tendency of a cancer that has resisted one drug to resist others that work the same way.
The receptor through which macrophages receive their main survival and differentiation signal, and a drug target for reducing or reprogramming them.
A chemokine made by activated fibroblasts and stellate cells that attracts and holds T cells, implicated in keeping them away from pancreatic cancer cells.
An abundant cell protein that daraxonrasib borrows as a partner to form the complex that blocks RAS.
The enzyme that inactivates gemcitabine; lower levels mean more active drug inside a cell.
A signaling protein released by tumor or immune cells that acts on distant organs, including the brain.
A systemic inflammatory reaction, with fever and low blood pressure, caused by large numbers of immune cells activating at once.
Examination of loose cells, here from fluid washed through the abdominal cavity, for cancer.
A T cell marked by CD8 that inspects protein fragments displayed on other cells and kills a cell showing something it recognizes as abnormal.
Loss of fitness and muscle from inactivity, which makes ordinary tasks more tiring.
A clot in a deep vein, usually of the leg, causing swelling and pain.
A clot in a deep vein, most often in the leg, causing one-sided swelling and pain.
The main treatment of a cancer when an operation is not planned.
A slow-to-empty stomach after pancreatic surgery, needing a tube or a liquid diet beyond the first week.
Removing or destroying the nerve supply to a tissue.
The enzyme that adds the first phosphate to gemcitabine, the step that activates it.
The dense, scar-like tissue reaction that the body builds in and around a tumor, which makes up most of the bulk of a pancreatic cancer.
How closely the cancer cells resemble normal cells; poorly differentiated tumors look least like their tissue of origin.
Hindered movement of water molecules on MRI, typical of tissue packed with cells such as a metastasis.
An MRI sequence that is bright where water molecules are hindered by densely packed cells and dark where they move freely.
An anticoagulant tablet, such as apixaban or rivaroxaban, that blocks one clotting enzyme directly.
The time after treatment during which no recurrence is detected.
The body and tail of the pancreas, the half that lies to the left of the vein crossing.
Removal of the body and tail of the pancreas, usually with the spleen when done for cancer.
Cancer reappearing in an organ away from the original site, such as the liver, lung or peritoneum.
A brief routine questionnaire asking about emotional, practical and physical problems at clinic visits.
Deficient mismatch repair, the loss of the proofreading system, detected by staining or testing.
A chemical tag on cytosine that, at a gene's promoter, switches the gene off.
A state in which disseminated cancer cells survive without dividing, sometimes for years, before resuming growth.
The cluster of sensory nerve-cell bodies beside the spinal cord where platinum drugs accumulate.
Postponing the next chemotherapy cycle to let blood counts or other side effects recover.
The share of the planned chemotherapy dose actually delivered over the planned time.
Delaying, reducing or stopping a chemotherapy drug to limit a side effect while continuing treatment.
Dilatation of both the bile duct and the pancreatic duct on imaging, which points to a blockage where the two converge in the head.
Simultaneous widening of the bile duct and pancreatic duct on a scan, usually from a blockage in the head of the pancreas.
A cut through both strands of the DNA helix, the lesion most likely to cause chromosome rearrangement if misrepaired.
A change in a tumor's category after treatment, which on scans happens far less often than clearance of the margin does.
An older name for SMAD4, short for 'deleted in pancreatic cancer 4'.
Reduced or absent activity of the DPD enzyme, which makes standard fluoropyrimidine doses dangerous.
The gene for DPD, the enzyme that breaks down fluorouracil and capecitabine; reduced-function versions cause drug build-up.
The lymph node that collects fluid from a region of the body and where T-cell responses to anything arriving there are started.
The cell lining the pancreatic ducts, whose appearance the cancer resembles.
An abrupt interruption of the pancreatic duct on a scan, usually at the site of a tumor, with dilatation upstream.
The main pancreatic duct, which runs the length of the gland and opens at the ampulla.
An antidepressant that also reduces nerve pain, used off-label for painful chemotherapy neuropathy.
Cramps, sweating and faintness after meals when food enters the small bowel too quickly.
The first part of the small intestine, which wraps around the head of the pancreas.
An unpleasant abnormal sensation such as tingling or burning triggered by touch or cold.
Feeling full after only a few mouthfuls.
A short scale on which patients rate the severity of nine common symptoms.
The epidermal growth factor receptor, a protein on the cell surface that feeds growth signals into the RAS pathway.
A laboratory test that counts individual immune cells secreting a signaling protein after being shown a specific target.
Likely to cause nausea and vomiting; chemotherapy drugs are ranked by this risk.
Bacteria with a protective outer coat, such as pneumococcus, that the spleen is especially important for clearing.
Tumor surrounding more than half the circumference of a blood vessel on a scan.
The hormone-making part of the pancreas, the islets, which release insulin and glucagon directly into the blood.
An ultrasound probe on the tip of an endoscope that images the pancreas from inside the stomach or duodenum.
A naturally occurring fragment of a matrix protein that inhibits the growth of new blood vessels.
A distant regulatory DNA switch that sets how strongly a gene is expressed in a given cell type.
A capsule coating that resists stomach acid and dissolves in the small intestine.
A shift in which an organized, sheet-forming cell takes on the looser, more mobile character of a connective-tissue cell.
An endoscopic procedure that reaches the bile duct through the mouth and stomach to place a stent or clear a blockage.
An endoscopic procedure that creates an internal connection between the stomach and small bowel using a short wide stent.
The part of the pancreas that makes digestive enzymes and bicarbonate and sends them into the intestine through ducts.
Too little pancreatic enzyme reaching the intestine to digest food.
Too little pancreatic enzyme reaching the small intestine to digest fat, protein and starch.
A small membrane-bound packet of protein and RNA released by a cell and taken up by other cells.
A result a trial looks at without being designed to test it, so a difference found there raises a question rather than answering one.
A set of genes a cell switches on together, describing what the cell is currently doing rather than its fixed identity.
Removal of lymph node stations beyond the standard field, practiced in some centers but not shown to improve survival.
The mesh of proteins and sugars that cells secrete around themselves to give tissue its structure and stiffness.
A questionnaire scoring appetite and cachexia symptoms from the patient's point of view.
A quality-of-life questionnaire designed for people with liver, bile-duct and pancreatic cancers.
The clotting enzyme that apixaban and rivaroxaban block.
Death following a complication that might have been survived with earlier recognition and treatment.
A family with two or more first-degree relatives affected, often with no identified causative gene.
The enzyme that attaches a lipid tail to certain proteins, including RAS, so they can anchor to the inside of the cell membrane.
Vitamins A, D, E and K, which are absorbed with dietary fat and run low when fat is not digested.
Fluorodeoxyglucose, a radioactive sugar that accumulates in cells with high glucose use and is imaged by PET.
Fever occurring while the neutrophil count is low; treated as a medical emergency.
A stool test that measures a pancreatic enzyme as a marker of how much the gland is producing.
A form of cell death caused by uncontrolled oxidation of the fats in a cell's membranes.
Drawing loose cells into a thin needle for a cytologist to examine.
Cutting a small core of tissue with a needle so that the tissue's structure is preserved.
The proportion of a defined group still alive five years after diagnosis or treatment.
A chemotherapy drug that mimics the RNA base uracil and blocks the enzyme that makes the DNA base thymine.
A four-drug chemotherapy combination of folinic acid (leucovorin), fluorouracil, irinotecan and oxaliplatin given every two weeks.
One session of a radiation course.
An open operation begun with the intention of removing the tumor but abandoned because spread is found.
A planned look at a trial's data partway through, which can stop the trial if the experimental treatment clearly will not prove better.
Granulocyte colony-stimulating factor, an injected growth factor that speeds recovery of neutrophils after chemotherapy.
A KRAS variant with approved drugs in lung and bowel cancer but found in only 1 to 3 percent of pancreatic cancers.
The commonest KRAS mutation in pancreatic cancer, replacing glycine with aspartate at position 12 and jamming the switch on.
The metal in MRI contrast agents, which brightens tissues according to their blood supply.
A new activity acquired by a mutated protein, beyond the loss of its normal role.
A cluster of nerve cell bodies outside the brain and spinal cord; the celiac ganglia are the largest in the abdomen.
Blockage of the duodenum that stops the stomach emptying, causing vomiting of old food.
Enlarged veins in the stomach wall that carry rerouted blood when the splenic vein is blocked and may bleed.
A branch of the hepatic artery that runs down between the head and neck of the pancreas and supplies the head and duodenum.
A surgical bypass joining the stomach directly to the jejunum so food can skip a blocked duodenum.
A transcription factor that maintains the classical program; its loss marks the basal-like state.
Growth differentiation factor 15, a stress signal released by tumors that suppresses appetite and activity through a brainstem receptor.
Growth differentiation factor 15, a stress signal released by tumors that affects appetite, activity and, in this setting, pain.
An abnormal joining of two genes that can create a permanently active growth-signaling protein.
A failed division that leaves a cell with two complete sets of chromosomes, after which losses are better tolerated.
Latin for knee; the bend the pancreas makes as its neck rises over the portal vein.
Inherited and present in every cell of the body, detectable in a blood or saliva test.
Sequencing of blood or saliva to find inherited variants present in every cell.
A gene change inherited from a parent and present in every cell of the body, as distinct from one acquired by the tumor.
The stomach's hunger hormone, which anamorelin imitates to stimulate appetite and growth-hormone release.
A hormone from islet alpha cells that raises blood sugar by releasing glucose from the liver.
A natural signal that recruits and matures the cells which present antigens, used in whole-cell vaccines to draw the immune system to the injection site.
A pathologist's score of how abnormal cancer cells look, from well differentiated (resembling normal cells) to poorly differentiated.
A US Preventive Services Task Force rating that a service should not be offered because harms outweigh benefits.
A protein secreted by macrophages in the liver that activates hepatic stellate cells into a scar-forming state supporting metastatic growth.
A small protein released by one cell that tells a neighboring cell to grow or divide by binding a receptor on its surface.
The small energy-carrying molecule whose binding switches RAS on; its conversion to GDP switches RAS off.
Methyl tags on lysine 9 of histone H3 that mark tightly packed, silenced chromatin.
Redness, soreness and peeling of the palms and soles caused by capecitabine and some infusional fluorouracil schedules.
The ratio of event rates between two groups over the whole follow-up; 0.70 means a 30% lower rate in the treated group.
A blood test reflecting average blood sugar over about three months.
A signaling route by which tumor cells instruct surrounding fibroblasts to build stroma.
A common benign tangle of blood vessels in the liver that fills slowly with contrast from the edge inward.
Removal of about half the pancreas, as in living-donor pancreas transplantation.
A liver cell that stores vitamin A at rest and becomes a scar-forming myofibroblast when activated.
A late set of images with a liver-specific contrast agent in which normal liver cells take up the agent and metastases do not.
The fold of tissue between the liver and duodenum that carries the portal vein, hepatic artery and bile duct.
A receptor on the cell surface that, when stimulated by neuregulin, pairs with HER2 to drive growth.
Genetic variation between different cells or regions of the same tumor.
Severely disordered precursor cells still confined to the duct, also called carcinoma in situ.
A hospital that performs many pancreatic operations each year, which is associated with lower operative mortality.
The notch on an organ where its blood vessels enter and leave; the pancreatic tail reaches the hilum of the spleen.
The spool proteins around which DNA is wound, carrying chemical tags that mark regions as active or silent.
The tissue-type molecules that hold up protein fragments from inside a cell so T cells can inspect them; people carry different versions.
The accurate repair of a double-strand break using the matching sister copy of the chromosome as a template.
Loss of both copies of a stretch of DNA, so the gene is physically absent rather than misspelled.
Care focused entirely on comfort in the final phase of illness, after disease-directed treatment stops.
Homologous recombination deficiency, the functional loss of accurate double-strand-break repair.
A long sugar chain in the matrix that binds large amounts of water, making the tissue swell and press outward.
A low blood potassium level, which on this regimen usually follows diarrhea and can affect heart rhythm.
Having fewer blood vessels than the surrounding tissue, which is how pancreatic cancer typically appears.
A shortage of oxygen in a tissue, which changes how its cells behave and which genes they switch on.
Inflammation of a normal organ caused by T cells released from their brakes.
An animal model with a working immune system, in which the immune contribution to a drug's effect can be seen.
Staining a tissue slide with antibodies to show whether a particular protein is present and where it sits.
A drug that binds KRAS only while it is in its switched-off, GDP-bound shape and keeps it there.
A spot on a scan whose nature the radiologist cannot decide from that scan alone.
The fibroblast state found further from the cancer cells, which secretes signaling molecules such as interleukin-6 rather than building matrix.
A small portable device that delivers fluorouracil slowly over 46 hours through a central line while the person is at home.
Analysing every patient in the group they were assigned to, whether or not they completed the planned treatment.
Analysing everyone as assigned at randomization whether or not they took the treatment, which preserves the fairness of the comparison.
A look at a trial's data before enrollment is complete, which can give a more favorable number than the final one.
A segment of vein or synthetic tube used to bridge the gap when a long vein segment is removed.
The pressure in the fluid between cells, which can collapse small blood vessels when it exceeds the pressure inside them.
Inflammation of the lung tissue between the air sacs, a rare serious side effect of gemcitabine.
The pressure in the fluid and gel between cells, which in a tumor can rise high enough to squeeze its own blood vessels shut.
A cancer that appears, often advanced, between scheduled surveillance visits.
Image-guided procedures such as placing a drain or blocking a bleeding artery without open surgery.
Intraductal papillary mucinous neoplasm, a mucus-producing cystic growth in a pancreatic duct that can occasionally develop an invasive cancer.
A microscopic cluster of hormone-producing cells within the pancreas that releases insulin and glucagon into the blood.
Clusters of hormone-producing cells scattered through the pancreas, including the beta cells that make insulin.
Clusters of hormone-producing cells scattered through the pancreas that release insulin and glucagon into the blood.
Having the same density as the surrounding gland on CT, so the tumor casts no visible shadow.
The part of the small intestine after the duodenum, to which the stomach and pancreas are reconnected after a Whipple.
A graph of the proportion of a group surviving over time that accounts for patients still alive at the time of analysis.
A 0 to 100 scale of day-to-day function, where 70 means able to care for oneself but unable to work.
A points system for clot risk in cancer patients; pancreatic cancer alone scores 2, the high-risk threshold.
An enzyme that adds phosphate groups to other proteins to switch signaling pathways on.
A gene whose protein relays growth signals; a mutation that locks it on is the first step in nearly every pancreatic cancer.
A version of the KRAS protein in which the amino acid at position 12 has changed from glycine to cysteine, found in about 1 to 3 percent of pancreatic cancers.
A version of the KRAS protein in which the amino acid at position 12 has changed from glycine to aspartic acid, the commonest KRAS mutation in pancreatic cancer.
A tumor whose KRAS gene has no mutation, found in about one in ten pancreatic cancers.
A macrophage that lives in the liver's blood channels and filters what arrives in portal blood.
A way of counting survival from a later fixed time point so that patients are not credited for simply having lived long enough to be measured.
Diarrhea beginning more than a day after an irinotecan dose, caused by SN-38 released in the gut.
The interval by which one test detects a change before another test does.
The apparent lengthening of survival that comes simply from diagnosing a cancer earlier, without delaying death.
Body weight minus fat, used in cachexia trials as a measure of muscle.
High pressure confined to the splenic venous system when the splenic vein is blocked, with a normal liver and open portal vein.
The thin pocket of the abdominal lining between the back of the stomach and the front of the pancreas.
A form of folate, also called folinic acid, given with fluorouracil to lock the drug onto its target enzyme.
Lacking the blood-group enzyme needed to make CA 19-9, so the marker stays low regardless of tumor burden.
The position of a regimen in the order of treatments for advanced cancer, so that first line is the initial regimen and second line is the one given after it stops working.
A technique that permanently labels one cell type so its descendants, including any tumor, can be identified.
The pancreatic enzyme that breaks dietary fat into absorbable pieces.
A drug enclosed in a tiny fat bubble so that it circulates longer and is released slowly.
Irinotecan wrapped in microscopic fat bubbles that keep it circulating longer, sold as Onivyde.
A microscopic bubble of fat molecules used to carry a drug through the bloodstream and release it slowly.
Keeping the tumor from growing in the place it was treated, as distinct from preventing spread elsewhere.
Cancer reappearing in the area where the original tumor was removed.
A tumor that encases an artery or blocks the main vein so that removal with a clear margin is not expected, without distant spread.
An over-the-counter drug that slows the bowel, used at the first loose stool for late irinotecan diarrhea.
The loss of the second, working copy of a gene in a cell that started with one faulty copy.
Mildly disordered but orderly-looking precursor cells that are extremely common and rarely progress.
An injected anticoagulant such as enoxaparin, long the standard for clots in cancer.
The number of positive nodes divided by the number examined; a ratio above 0.2 predicts early recurrence.
A numbered anatomical group of lymph nodes, such as those behind the pancreatic head or along the superior mesenteric artery.
The number of cancer-containing lymph nodes divided by the number examined, a predictor of early recurrence.
Chemotherapy given before an infusion of engineered cells to clear space for them, which predictably lowers blood counts.
An inherited loss of one mismatch-repair gene copy that raises the risk of several cancers.
The acidic compartment inside a cell where delivered material is cut back into its component parts.
A long-lived myeloid cell that swallows debris and dying cells, displays fragments of them to T cells, and helps direct tissue repair.
Bulk drinking: a cell throws out a ruffle of membrane, closes it around a gulp of surrounding fluid, and digests whatever protein was dissolved in it.
A gentler treatment continued after a response to hold the cancer in check.
Treatment given to hold disease in check after initial chemotherapy has controlled it.
Bleeding that lowers hemoglobin by 2 g/dL or more, needs transfusion, or occurs in a critical site such as the brain.
A state in which intake or absorption falls short of the body's needs, measured by weight loss, intake and muscle.
The RAF-MEK-ERK relay that carries a RAS signal to the nucleus and turns on growth genes.
The cut edge of a removed specimen; a clear (R0) margin means no cancer cells are found at the edge, which does not by itself mean the cancer is cured.
An operation in which no tumor is found at the cut edges of the removed specimen; it improves the odds but does not mean cure.
An operation after which the pathologist finds no cancer at the cut edges of the specimen, also called R0.
An immune cell that releases histamine and other inflammatory chemicals, found clustered around nerves in painful tumors.
Mucinous cystic neoplasm, a mucin-filled cyst with ovarian-type wall tissue, usually in the body or tail and almost always in women.
The enzyme that keeps p53 levels low in healthy cells by tagging it for destruction.
The middle value of a group: the time by which half of the patients have reached the event and half have not.
The time by which half of a defined group of patients has died and half is still alive.
A kinase immediately downstream of RAS that passes the growth signal along to ERK.
A protein found on the surface of most pancreatic cancer cells and little normal tissue, which made it an early immune target.
The single layer of cells lining the peritoneum, pleura and pericardium, which makes MUC16.
A vaccine that delivers genetic instructions so the body's own cells briefly make the target protein and display it to the immune system.
A fall in tracer uptake after treatment, which can occur without any change in size.
The volume of tissue whose tracer uptake exceeds a chosen threshold.
The amount of tumor taking up radioactive sugar on a PET scan, which can fall before any change in size is visible.
A deposit of cancer growing in an organ distant from where it started.
A two-weekly regimen of oxaliplatin with infusional fluorouracil and leucovorin, borrowed from colorectal cancer.
The surface molecule, called HLA class I in people, that every nucleated cell uses to display short peptides from the proteins it is making.
A surface molecule that displays fragments of protein to CD4 T cells; immune cells normally carry it, and some tumor fibroblasts do too.
A deposit of cancer cells at a distant site too small to be seen on any scan.
A pattern of shifting lengths in short repeated DNA sequences that indicates mismatch repair has failed, used as the test for that state.
The pattern of errors in repetitive DNA that reveals a tumor has lost mismatch repair.
Protein filaments that form a cell's internal scaffolding and pull chromosomes apart during division; paclitaxel freezes them.
The number of small blood vessels per area of tumor tissue under the microscope.
Cancer cells that remain in the body after treatment has removed everything visible.
Surgery through small incisions using a camera and instruments, laparoscopic or robotic.
The proofreading system that corrects wrongly paired letters left behind after DNA copying.
Loss of the system that corrects copying errors in DNA, which leaves the cancer with large numbers of mutations and therefore many visible targets.
A single-letter change that swaps one amino acid for another, producing an altered rather than absent protein.
A version of FOLFIRINOX that drops the fluorouracil bolus and often lowers the irinotecan dose to make it easier to tolerate.
An MRI technique that shows the bile and pancreatic ducts as bright fluid-filled tubes without any contrast injection.
The very large mucin molecule whose shed fragment is measured as CA-125.
Acting on mutant and normal forms of several RAS proteins, rather than on one specific mutation.
Involving several medical specialties working together on one patient's care.
A solid lump on the inner wall of a cyst, a feature that raises concern on imaging.
A characteristic pattern of DNA changes that reveals which process, such as aging or failed repair, produced them.
An immature myeloid cell that accumulates in cancer and actively blunts T-cell responses.
An activated fibroblast that both secretes collagen and contracts, pulling on the tissue around it.
The fibroblast state found pressed directly against cancer glands, which contracts and secretes most of the collagen.
The part of the staging system that counts cancer-containing lymph nodes: N0 none, N1 one to three, N2 four or more.
Paclitaxel bound to nanoparticles of the blood protein albumin, which replaces the castor-oil solvent of older paclitaxel.
The lowest point the blood count reaches after a chemotherapy dose, usually a week or two later.
The identifier a trial receives when registered on ClinicalTrials.gov, such as NCT06625320.
Cancer cells carried along the path of a biopsy needle and left behind in the tissue it passed through.
The proportion of people with a negative test who truly do not have the condition being tested for.
Treatment given before the main treatment, usually chemotherapy before surgery.
Chemotherapy or radiation given before an operation rather than after it.
A peptide created by a mutation in the cancer, and therefore one that no healthy cell in the body displays.
A tumor-cell gene program resembling immature nerve tissue, found enriched in tumors removed after chemotherapy and radiotherapy.
A tumor arising from hormone-producing islet-type cells of the pancreas, usually slower-growing than ductal adenocarcinoma.
Deliberately destroying a nerve or nerve plexus with alcohol or another agent to stop it carrying pain.
A growth factor, such as nerve growth factor, that nerve fibers need to survive and extend.
A neutrophil count low enough, usually below 500 per microliter, that ordinary infections become dangerous.
The most common white blood cell, the first line of defense against bacteria.
Diabetes appearing for the first time, which after middle age can be an early sign of an occult pancreatic cancer.
High-throughput reading of many genes at once to catalog a tumor's DNA changes.
A statement that a test found no detectable cancer, which does not exclude disease below the test's limit of detection.
A homologous-recombination-related gene other than BRCA1, BRCA2 or PALB2, generally conferring weaker drug sensitivity.
A person whose CA 19-9 stays undetectable even with cancer present, usually because of Lewis-negative genotype.
A trial designed to show that a new approach is not worse than the standard by more than a pre-set margin, rather than better.
A fall of a tumor marker back into the reference range after treatment.
A report phrase meaning the tumor's edge has blurred into treated tissue so that no discrete mass can be measured.
The gene for neuregulin, a growth factor that activates HER3; when fused, it keeps that receptor constantly stimulated.
A fusion involving the NRG1 gene that activates HER-family receptors and is targetable with zenocutuzumab in pancreatic cancer.
A drug shaped like a DNA or RNA building block that cells mistakenly use, disrupting copying.
A tumor shrinking by a defined amount on imaging, which is a different measurement from living longer.
The percentage of people whose tumors shrink by a set amount on scans, which is not the same as living longer.
A deposit of cancer that exists but was not detected by the tests used.
A measure that approximates relative risk, comparing the odds of exposure in people with and without the disease.
A second-line regimen of oxaliplatin, folinic acid (leucovorin) and fluorouracil tested in the CONKO-003 trial.
Prescribing an approved drug for a use not listed on its label, which is legal and often guideline-supported.
The fatty apron of peritoneum hanging from the stomach, a common site for peritoneal deposits.
Resistance caused by a change in the drug's own binding site, so the drug can no longer attach to its target.
A gene that, when mutated or over-expressed, actively drives cell growth.
The permanent growth arrest a cell enters when a single activating mutation triggers the p16 and p53 stress responses.
A virus chosen or engineered to replicate inside cancer cells, killing them and alerting the immune system in the process.
A trial in which participants and clinicians know which treatment was assigned.
A drink or powder providing concentrated protein and calories between or with meals.
A small clump of cells grown in a gel so that it reproduces part of a tissue's three-dimensional structure in the laboratory.
The time from treatment start or randomization until death from any cause.
The protein made by CDKN2A that blocks CDK4 and CDK6 and keeps a stressed cell out of the division cycle.
The protein made by TP53 that halts a damaged cell, directs repair, or triggers its death or retirement.
The time until pain worsens by a set amount on a questionnaire or the person dies.
A core repair gene that bridges BRCA1 and BRCA2 in the double-strand-break repair relay.
Specialist care for symptoms, communication and decisions that runs alongside cancer treatment.
A CT scan with thin slices and contrast injection timed to show the pancreas, its arteries and its veins in separate phases.
A leak of enzyme-rich pancreatic juice from the join between the pancreas and the bowel after surgery.
A hormone made by cells concentrated in the uncinate process that rises after meals and is a marker of this region's function.
Fat within the pancreas, seen on CT as lower density than the spleen, which reduces the working capacity of the remnant.
A star-shaped cell that sits quietly in the normal pancreas storing fat and vitamin A and becomes the main scar-building cell when the organ is injured.
The closed cut end of the pancreas left after the body and tail are removed.
The formal name for the Whipple operation: removal of the pancreatic head and duodenum together.
The pharmaceutical mixture of lipase, protease and amylase from pig pancreas used in enzyme capsules.
Pancreatic intraepithelial neoplasia, a microscopic precursor lesion in a small duct that can, rarely, progress to cancer.
Lymph nodes beside the aorta, beyond the standard surgical field, whose involvement is generally treated as distant spread.
Caused by substances a tumor releases into the body rather than by its direct growth.
Diabetes caused by signals from a tumor rather than by loss of islets, which can improve when the tumor is removed.
An enzyme that detects single-strand breaks in DNA and recruits the proteins that repair them.
A drug that blocks a backup DNA-repair route, killing cells that already lack homologous recombination.
No living cancer cells found in the removed specimen after preoperative treatment.
Whether a cancer returns locally, at distant sites, or both after treatment.
A receptor on T cells that switches them off when engaged, which tumors exploit to escape attack.
Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma, the common form of pancreatic cancer, arising from duct-like cells of the exocrine pancreas.
A long-acting form of G-CSF given once per chemotherapy cycle rather than daily.
The proportion of people carrying a risk variant who actually develop the associated cancer.
A branch of glucose metabolism that makes building blocks for DNA and the antioxidant NADPH.
Standard criteria for scoring treatment response from changes in PET tracer uptake rather than size.
Draining the bile duct through a needle passed through the skin and liver when the endoscopic route fails.
A simple scale of how well a person can carry out daily activities, used to judge fitness for treatment.
Blood actually flowing through a tissue, as distinct from the number of blood vessels present in it.
Arising at the junction where the bile duct and pancreatic duct enter the duodenum; such cancers may be pancreatic, biliary, ampullary or duodenal.
Cancer cells growing along the sheath of a nerve.
Treatment given both before and after an operation.
A matrix protein secreted by activated stellate cells that helps build the fibrous tissue around a metastasis.
Nerve damage felt as numbness, tingling or pain, usually starting in the fingers and toes.
Cancer deposits scattered over the lining of the abdominal cavity, which can kink or narrow the bowel.
Saline rinsed over the abdominal lining and collected so that any free cancer cells can be found under the microscope.
The thin membrane lining the abdominal cavity and covering its organs.
A measurement showing a drug did what it was designed to do in the body, which is a separate question from whether patients lived longer.
A measurement showing a drug changed the biology it was aimed at, which is separate from showing the patient did better.
The study of how inherited gene variants change a person's response to, and handling of, drugs.
An early trial that finds a safe dose and records side effects in a small number of patients.
A trial that tests whether a treatment shows activity, usually without a randomized comparison.
A large randomized trial comparing a new treatment with the current standard, usually with survival as the endpoint.
A large randomized trial designed to show whether a treatment works well enough to be approved.
The second main RAS output, through PI3K, AKT and mTOR, which boosts nutrient uptake and protein synthesis and suppresses cell death.
The ability of a cancer cell to change its gene program in response to its surroundings without changing its DNA.
A platinum atom chemically bonded to DNA bases, distorting the helix and blocking copying.
Drugs such as oxaliplatin or cisplatin that cross-link DNA strands, which cells lacking homologous recombination cannot repair.
A person whose inherited enzyme versions clear a drug slowly, reaching higher and more toxic levels.
The large vein that carries blood from the intestine, pancreas and spleen to the liver.
An analysis decided after the data were seen, which can find differences that a planned analysis would not.
Outcome data entered into the trial registry itself, which many published trials never provide.
A leak of enzyme-rich pancreatic juice from the cut surface or join of the pancreas after surgery.
Bleeding after pancreatic surgery, classed as early or late, into the gut or abdomen, mild or severe.
Changes in a distant organ, induced by the primary tumor before any cancer cells arrive, that make it more hospitable to metastasis.
Exercise and nutrition before an operation to improve fitness for surgery.
The FDA pathway for high-risk medical devices, separate from the drug-approval process.
A hormone-like drug such as megestrol used in short courses to stimulate appetite.
Growth of the cancer or appearance of new spots on scans, or clear clinical worsening, that marks the end of a regimen's usefulness.
The time from treatment start until the cancer grows on scans or the patient dies, whichever comes first.
An acid-suppressing drug added when enzymes alone give an incomplete response, because acid destroys lipase.
The medical word for itching.
Psychological and psychiatric care specialized for people with cancer and their families.
A clot that has travelled to the lungs, causing breathlessness and chest pain.
A classifier that assigns classical or basal-like subtype from a small set of tumor-specific genes.
The muscular valve at the outlet of the stomach that controls emptying into the duodenum.
A variant of the operation that keeps the stomach's outlet valve.
The resting, non-activated state a cell can be pushed back into instead of being killed.
A resection in which no tumor is found at the inked edges of the specimen, which does not mean no cancer remains in the body.
Surgical removal in which no cancer cells are found at the cut edges of the specimen; it does not by itself mean cure.
A resection in which tumor lies at or within 1 millimeter of an inked edge of the specimen.
Radical antegrade modular pancreatosplenectomy, a deeper right-to-left dissection designed to clear the back margin and lymph nodes.
A family of switch proteins (KRAS, NRAS, HRAS) that are on when bound to GTP and off when bound to GDP, relaying growth signals into the cell.
Any mutation at position 12 of a RAS protein, the group in which the pivotal trial's endpoints were defined.
A drug that blocks the RAS proteins whose mutant form drives most pancreatic cancers.
A drug that binds RAS in its active, signal-sending state rather than its resting state.
The retinoblastoma protein, a brake that holds a cell out of the division cycle until CDK4/6 releases it.
A standard way of measuring tumor response on scans from changes in the diameters of chosen lesions.
The time from a starting point, usually surgery, until cancer is detected again or the person dies, whichever comes first.
Blockage of a stent by sludge, tumor or displacement so that jaundice returns and a further procedure is needed.
The public record of a trial's design, eligibility and enrollment status, created before the trial starts and updated as it runs.
A T cell whose job is to suppress other immune cells, useful for preventing autoimmunity and unhelpful when it suppresses an anti-tumor response.
The share of the planned drug dose over the planned time that a person actually received.
How many times more common a disease is in people with a factor than in people without it.
The portion of pancreas left in place after a partial resection.
The part of the pancreas left in place after surgery.
A common variant in which the artery to the right liver arises from the superior mesenteric artery and runs under the pancreatic head.
Judged from scans to be removable by surgery with a clear margin, based on vessel contact and absence of spread.
The proportion of patients whose measured tumors shrink by a set amount on scans.
Repeating scans and blood tests after a period of treatment to see whether the extent of disease has changed.
Lying behind the peritoneal lining of the abdomen, where the pancreas, aorta and major vessels sit.
The space behind the abdominal lining and in front of the spine where the pancreas, aorta and celiac plexus lie.
The enzyme that makes the deoxynucleotide building blocks of DNA, which gemcitabine inhibits.
Something that raises the average chance of a disease across a population without causing it in any one person.
Reading the tumor's RNA messages, which detects fusions that DNA-only panels can miss.
Low skeletal muscle mass, usually measured on a CT scan.
The support cell that wraps peripheral nerve fibers and helps them grow or repair.
The treatment given after the first regimen has stopped controlling the cancer.
A hormone released by the duodenum in response to acid that tells duct cells to secrete bicarbonate.
The way a group's definition, such as trial eligibility or reaching surgery, shapes its survival figures independently of treatment.
A mesh tube placed by endoscopy that springs open to hold a duct or bowel segment open.
A wire-mesh tube that springs open inside the bile duct to a wide bore and stays open longer than plastic.
A permanent exit from the division cycle that a damaged or oncogene-stressed cell can enter instead of dying.
A small, self-limiting bleed that can warn of a major arterial bleed to come.
An acute-phase protein made by liver cells during inflammation that attracts immune cells.
A target present in many different people's tumors, which allows one vaccine to be made in advance rather than built per patient.
An enzyme that relays signals from surface receptors toward RAS, acting just upstream of it.
A study in which everyone receives the treatment, so outcomes can only be compared with expectation rather than with a control group.
A trial in which everyone receives the treatment, so results cannot be compared with an untreated group drawn at the same time.
A method that reads which genes are active in each cell nucleus separately, usable on frozen tissue.
A functional test measuring how far a person can walk in six minutes.
Muscle area on a CT slice at the third lumbar vertebra divided by height squared.
The cut surface of a Whipple specimen facing the superior mesenteric artery, the margin most often found to contain cancer.
The shared relay protein without which TGF-β signals cannot reach the nucleus; also called DPC4.
The active form of irinotecan, made in the body, that traps topoisomerase I on DNA.
Arising in the tumor only, detectable by testing tumor tissue but not blood.
Sequencing of the tumor itself to find alterations it has acquired.
A protein that helps load RAS with GTP, the step that switches RAS on.
A transcription factor that maintains duct-cell identity and is required for acinar cells to reprogram into a duct-like state.
A protein in tumor stroma once thought to pull albumin-bound drugs into the tumor, a role that later studies did not confirm.
Measuring gene activity in small defined regions of tissue so that the position of each measurement is preserved.
The ring of muscle at the ampulla that controls the release of bile and pancreatic juice.
The nerves that carry sympathetic and pain fibers between the celiac plexus and the spinal cord.
Surgical removal of the spleen.
The branch of the celiac axis that winds along the top of the pancreatic body and tail to the spleen.
The notch in the spleen where its artery and vein enter and where the tail of the pancreas ends.
The vein that runs along the back of the pancreatic body and tail from the spleen to the portal vein.
A molecular type of pancreatic cancer, defined by gene activity patterns, that is more frequent in body and tail tumors and behaves aggressively.
A keyhole operation to look inside the abdomen for small deposits of cancer that scans cannot see.
A number describing how concentrated the tracer is in a region relative to the dose and body size.
A named version of a drug-metabolism gene, such as UGT1A1*28, defining its activity level.
Pale, greasy, floating stools caused by undigested fat.
The resting fibroblast-like cell of the pancreas that stores fat droplets and becomes activated into a matrix-producing cell by injury or cancer.
A small mesh or plastic tube placed inside a blocked duct to hold it open.
Radiation given in a few large, precisely aimed doses, usually five, with imaging to keep the beam off nearby bowel.
The dense, scar-like supporting tissue of fibroblasts, matrix and immune cells that surrounds pancreatic cancer cells.
A population of tumor cells descended from one ancestor that carries its own private set of mutations.
The artery from the aorta that supplies the small intestine and right colon, passing behind the pancreatic neck and in front of the uncinate process.
The vein that drains the small intestine and right colon and passes behind the pancreatic neck.
Regular imaging of people at high risk to find cancer early, distinct from screening the general public.
The groove on the RAS protein where several KRAS drugs attach; mutations there can block the drug from binding.
An experimental step that removes T cells with antibodies to test whether they are needed for an effect.
The natural receptor a T cell uses to read short protein fragments displayed by a tissue-type molecule on another cell's surface.
Direct evidence that a drug actually reached and acted on the molecule it was designed to hit, measured separately from whether the patient improved.
The stable three-part grouping of drug, enzyme and folate that keeps thymidylate synthase blocked.
A signaling protein that drives fibroblasts towards the contractile, collagen-making state and suppresses the inflammatory one.
Transforming growth factor beta, a secreted signal that restrains epithelial growth and instructs fibroblasts to make scar tissue.
The enzyme that makes thymidylate, the thymine building block of DNA, and the target of fluorouracil.
An approval that applies to any cancer carrying a specified molecular feature, regardless of the organ it started in.
A drug approval based on a molecular alteration regardless of where the cancer started.
The staging shorthand for tumor size (T), lymph node involvement (N) and distant metastasis (M).
An enzyme that cuts and reseals one DNA strand to relieve twisting during copying; irinotecan traps it mid-cut.
Giving all planned chemotherapy and radiation before surgery rather than splitting it around the operation.
Removal of the entire pancreas, usually with the duodenum, bile duct, gallbladder and spleen.
The adhesive pad containing electrodes that is stuck to the skin to deliver the fields.
The three-part assembly of drug, cyclophilin A and RAS that these inhibitors form to block signaling.
A regular meeting at which specializts from surgery, oncology, radiology and pathology review each patient's case together and agree a plan.
The fraction of a sample that is cancer cells rather than scar, blood or normal tissue.
A substance measurable in blood whose level tends to track the amount of cancer present.
The total number of mutations in a tumor, raised sharply when mismatch repair is lost.
A pathologist's estimate of how much of a treated tumor is scar rather than living cancer.
Low-intensity alternating electric fields delivered through skin arrays, intended to disrupt dividing cells in the treated region.
A macrophage inside a tumor, usually in a state that supports tissue building and suppresses T cells rather than one that attacks the cancer.
A ctDNA test designed around mutations first found by sequencing the patient's own tumor.
The fraction of a vessel’s circumference that the tumor touches on a CT scan.
The antigen-presenting cell that starts CD8 T-cell responses, and without which the protective fibroblast effect disappears.
Diabetes caused by disease or removal of the pancreas, as distinct from type 1 or type 2.
The gene for the enzyme that clears irinotecan's active metabolite; low-activity variants raise toxicity.
A hook-shaped extension of the pancreatic head that curls behind the superior mesenteric vein.
The main parasympathetic nerve to the abdominal organs, carrying cholinergic signals to the pancreas.
Enlarged veins in the wall of the stomach or esophagus that can bleed when blood is rerouted around a blocked vein.
A signaling protein released by oxygen-starved tissue that instructs nearby blood vessels to grow.
Cancer cells found within the wall of a resected vein under the microscope, as opposed to merely touching it.
A clot in a vein, usually a deep-vein thrombosis in the leg or a pulmonary embolism in the lung.
A clot in the veins draining the gut, liver or spleen, often found incidentally on scans.
A growth-promoting transcription co-activator that some tumors amplify to survive without KRAS.
The tumor stage assigned by the pathologist after preoperative treatment, the y marking that treatment came first.
Stage assigned from the surgical specimen after preoperative treatment, which may differ from the stage estimated before it.
Whether one or both copies of a gene are affected in a cell.
An inactive precursor form of a digestive enzyme that is switched on only after it reaches the intestine.
